Cisco Nexus 3000 and 9000 Series Switches NGOAM Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20Nexus%203000%20and%209000%20Series%20Switches%20NGOAM%20Remote%20Code%20Execution%20Vulnerabilities%26vs_k=1

Multiple vulnerabilities in the Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) feature of Cisco NX-OS Software, known as Next Generation OAM (NGOAM), could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges or cause a denial of service (DoS) condition on an affected device.
These vulnerabilities are due to improper input validation of IP traffic when NGOAM is enabled. An attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities by sending crafted packets to an IP interface on an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges and could cause process crashes, which could result in a reload of the device and a DoS condition.
Note: Feature requirements vary for each vulnerability. For details, see the Vulnerable Products (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20Nexus%203000%20and%209000%20Series%20Switches%20NGOAM%20Remote%20Code%20Execution%20Vulnerabilities%26vs_k=1#vp) section of this advisory.
Cisco has released software updates that address these vulnerabilities. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities.
This advisory is available at the following link:
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU
This advisory is part of a group of advisories. For a complete list of the advisories and links to them, see Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 7, 2026, Security Advisories (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-notice-fBn58ELx). For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco NX-OS Software, see Cisco NX-OS Software Security Hardening Release: October 2026 (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-hardening-nxosw1-cWzSbtR).

Javad Salehi Artimani, deputy for operations at Imam Khomeini Airport City, said the first Iraqi Airways flight arrived from Najaf at 7:30 a.m. Thursday and departed Tehran for Najaf at 8:30 a.m.
​
He said Iraqi Airways would operate one daily flight on the Tehran-Najaf route, with passenger services provided in both directions.
​
“The resumption of Iraqi Airways flights is a step toward the return and gradual expansion of foreign flights at the airport city, and we hope that, with conditions being provided, we will see an increase in the number of flights and the activation of more international routes,” Salehi Artimani said.
​
Iraqi Airways also announced the resumption of its direct flights from Najaf International Airport to Iran, with daily services to Tehran, Mashhad and Isfahan.
​
The airline said the move aims to facilitate passenger transportation and expand Iraq’s regional air links, particularly for religious, medical, and educational purposes.
​
Iraqi Airways suspended flights to Iran in early March amid the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran. The resumption followed Iraq’s efforts to secure a special exemption allowing the national carrier to operate flights to Iran.
​
The development comes after the Iraqi government also announced an agreement allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate up to 40 daily flights to and from Najaf International Airport.

An Ethereum Foundation researcher suggests pre-transferring large sums to addresses that have not yet signed any transactions

On October 7th, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake called on the crypto industry to calmly prepare for a scenario in which the ECDSA signature scheme could be hacked before the advent of a quantum computer. In his estimation, in the worst case, this could be a matter of months, not years. There is no confirmed method for such a hack.

Drake described the hack as rapid recovery of a private key from an already disclosed public one: for example, in about a week with available hardware such as a large cluster of graphics processors. According to him, it is now reasonable to prepare for such a possibility. He linked the warning to recent progress in mathematical models, including the publication of a set of mathematical works by OpenAI's internal model. The main risk, according to Drake, concerns addresses that have already signed transactions and thus revealed their public key. He recommends that large and prepared holders transfer most of their funds to addresses that have not signed anything yet. After each outgoing transaction, it is also better to transfer the remainder to a new address. You don't need a new wallet for this: you can get the address from the same seed phrase.

Drake specifically asks not to rush. According to him, there is cause for action, but a hasty transfer can do more harm than good. For wallets with less than 50 bitcoins, he sees partial coverage in already disclosed Satoshi addresses: around 20 thousand addresses with 50 bitcoins each. For oracle operators and second-layer network security advisors, he recommends changing the ECDSA key after each signed message or supplementing the signature with a hash-based scheme, such as SPHINCS.

According to his estimation, one can only exit this regime with cryptography designed for the period after the current development of artificial intelligence. Drake himself leans towards hash-based schemes and moving away from cryptography that relies on elliptic curves, lattices, or isogenies. In November, he plans to discuss the topic with institutional participants at a meeting in London.
